articles.title: X was supposed to be a bank by now
articles.summary: When he bought Twitter for $44 billion two years ago, Elon Musk said he wanted to turn the social network into an “everything app.” So far, X hasn’t achieved that vision.
articles.body: When Elon Musk was forced to buy Twitter two years ago, he said his goal was to turn the platform into two things: the “digital town square” and the “everything app.” He has failed at both goals. X isn’t something that is upsetting “the far right and the far left equally,” Instead, it has become Musk’s political weapon. In fact, he may be so preoccupied with trying to get Donald Trump elected that he has forgotten that X was supposed to be a bank by now. This time last year, Musk said in an internal X meeting that it “would blow my mind” if the service couldn’t handle “someone’s entire financial life” by the end of 2024. The first step toward this vision is a Venmo-like payment feature that’s still in development. X says it has secured money transmitter licenses to process payments in 38 states, including California, but has yet to get approval in key states like New York. Musk’s history of owning X has been nothing but broken promises. According to his own words, X was also supposed to be a dating service, a viable LinkedIn alternative for recruiting, and a YouTube killer by now. He said he was going to get rid of bots, too. I get more spam in my DMs than I did before Musk owned Twitter, and foreign governments have recently used bots on X to stoke division around the US presidential election. In some cases, X’s creator program means people are literally getting paid to manipulate the platform. One likely reason X has executed so poorly in the last two years is that, as long as he still has a personal megaphone, Musk may not actually care about the future of the product anymore. Network effects are strong with social networks, and X has remained surprisingly active in certain tech circles. The AI community’s obsession with it continues to amaze me given that all they’re doing is giving free training data to Musk’s AI model, Grok. His new obsession is trying to compete with OpenAI, which he helped start and then abandoned right before it struck gold with ChatGPT. He’s already raising even more money for his rival firm behind Grok, xAI, at a valuation north of $40 billion, which, on paper, would make his AI startup worth meaningfully more than X itself. He’s raising money out of necessity: I’ve heard Musk has already spent the $6 billion he raised for xAI earlier this year and needs more to buy additional compute from Nvidia, which announced this week that he plans to add another 100,000 H100s at his Colossus supercomputer site in Memphis, Tennessee. He also needs more capital to compete with the steep compensation packages top AI researchers can get elsewhere. Musk’s focus on increasing the value of xAI has to sting a bit for X employees, who were told they would be able to sell their shares every six months like SpaceX insiders can. This has yet to happen once. Company insiders I’ve spoken to doubt it ever will. After only two years, it increasingly looks like Musk thinks of X not as a town square or an everything app but as his personal Fox News and source of training data. Earnings notes A few observations from a busy week of tech earnings: * My cluster is bigger than yours: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg made a point to mention that LLama 4 is training on more than 100,000 Nvidia H100s, which just happens to be the size of Elon Musk’s xAI supercomputer. Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon will collectively spend $200 billion on capital expenditures — the majority of which is going to developing AI — and have all warned that spending will go up next year. (The US government spent about $126 billion on infrastructure last year, by comparison.) When CEOs are bragging about how much compute they have, they mainly have one constituent in mind: the AI researchers they are trying to poach from their rivals. * The most expensive acquihire of all time: Google confirmed that it paid a staggering $2.7 billion to rehire Character.AI CEO Noam Shazeer, along with his cofounder and roughly 30 of their researchers. The tidbit was included in Google’s Q3 earnings paperwork under a section creatively titled “Business Combinations,” which mentions “$2.7 billion of goodwill and $413 million of intangible assets” associated with the deal. As I reported last week, Shazeer is now co-leading the Gemini team and working on a reasoning model. Despite Google entering into a “non-exclusive license” to use Character’s LLM, I’ve confirmed the Gemini team has no intention of using it. * A change in tone: It’s clear that Microsoft and OpenAI are disentangling. During Microsoft’s earnings call this week, CEO Satya Nadella mostly focused on the financial upside of the company’s investment and not its product partnership with OpenAI. OpenAI’s launch of web search in ChatGPT makes barely any mention of the fact that it’s powered by Bing. Then there’s the news that GitHub Copilot is now also offering access to Claude and Gemini. Here’s where I’ll just note that OpenAI can get out of its contract with Microsoft if it declares it has reached AGI, which Sam Altman is now saying is “achievable with current hardware.” * Still waiting for Alexa: As I reported back in March, Amazon has been working on its own foundational model to hopefully revive its Alexa line of devices. The plan was originally to have debuted this Alexa reboot by now, but Bloomberg reports that the announcement has been pushed to 2025 due to lackluster results internally. On Amazon’s earnings call this week, executives confirmed that Alexa will have its brains replaced with a new AI model “in the near future.” (Relatedly, my colleagues published a series of great stories this week looking at the last decade of the Alexa product line.) Overheard “I think Nvidia is undervalued.” – SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son is always entertaining to listen to. His recent appearance at the Future Investment Initiative forum in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is no exception. Fresh off investing hundreds of millions of dollars in OpenAI’s latest funding round, he says that $9 trillion of capital expenditures seems “very reasonable” for achieving AGI, which he estimates will also require more than 400 gigawatts of electricity. Job board Some interesting tech career moves you may have missed lately: * Jay Parikh, the exec who built much of early Facebook’s engineering culture and more recently was CEO of Lacework, is joining Microsoft’s senior leadership team. CEO Satya Nadella says, “We will share more on his role and focus in the next few months.” * Dave Burke, Google’s ex-Android engineering chief, is now the CTO of Arc, a biomedical research nonprofit. * Peter Stern, a former deputy of Apple’s Eddy Cue and recent executive at Ford, is now the CEO of Peloton. * Rachel Whetstone, Netflix’s head of communications, and Dean Garfield, Netflix’s policy chief, are leaving as the streamer looks for a head of global affairs to oversee both functions. More links * If you haven’t already, make sure to read The Verge’s guide to next week’s presidential election, which features the only endorsement you’ll read that mentions USB-C. * Huh: Apple is acquiring the Pixelmator image editor and buying a 20 percent stake in GlobalStar, its satellite service provider for the iPhone. * There’s new evidence of rampant wash trading on Polymarket. * OSI’s official definition of open-source AI has been published. (Sorry, Meta!) * Bluesky board member Mike Masnick writes about “the state of decentralized social media.” * ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming is officially China’s richest person. * Meta published new AI research on robotics. * Claude released a native app for Mac and Windows. articles.title: IA e Relações Internacionais: como são os novos cursos da Unicamp | G1
articles.standfirst: As graduações serão oferecidas no campus de Limeira (SP) a partir do Vestibular 2027. Veja o que os estudantes vão aprender, como será a formação e quais são as possibilidades de atuação profissional.
articles.summary: Unicamp Vestibular 2027 oferece novas graduações em Inteligência Artificial e Relações Internacionais em Limeira, com foco em tecnologia e desafios globais.
articles.body:
A Unicamp estreia dois cursos de graduação no Vestibular 2027 : Inteligência Artificial e Ciência de Dados e Relações Internacionais, ambos oferecidos no campus de Limeira (SP).

Com propostas interdisciplinares, as novas graduações foram estruturadas para formar profissionais capazes de lidar com desafios contemporâneos em diferentes setores da sociedade.

Enquanto o primeiro curso combina conhecimentos de matemática, estatística e computação para desenvolver soluções baseadas em dados , o segundo reúne áreas como ciência política, economia e direito para analisar as relações entre países, empresas e organizações .

A criação das graduações é a principal novidade do processo seletivo para 2027, cuja primeira fase está marcada para o dia 18 de outubro . A seguir, o g1 apresenta um raio-x dos dois cursos, com detalhes sobre o que os estudantes vão aprender, como será a formação e possibilidades de atuação.

Inteligência Artificial e Ciência de Dados: da programação à criação de sistemas inteligentes

Oferecido em conjunto pela Faculdade de Ciências Aplicadas (FCA) e pela Faculdade de Tecnologia (FT), o bacharelado em Inteligência Artificial e Ciência de Dados tem como objetivo formar profissionais capazes de transformar dados em conhecimento, apoiar decisões e desenvolver soluções para problemas complexos .

A proposta vai além do uso de ferramentas prontas de inteligência artificial. Os estudantes terão uma formação voltada à compreensão dos algoritmos e modelos que sustentam essas tecnologias, à análise de diferentes tipos de dados e ao desenvolvimento de sistemas inteligentes.

De acordo com a Unicamp, o curso também aborda os impactos do uso da inteligência artificial, com discussões sobre ética, privacidade, vieses e responsabilidade . A ideia é preparar profissionais que não apenas desenvolvam tecnologias, mas também sejam capazes de avaliar suas possibilidades e consequências.

A grade curricular combina fundamentos teóricos e aplicações práticas. Entre os conteúdos previstos estão:

Matemática e estatística: fundamentos para compreender modelos, probabilidades e métodos de análise de dados.

Computação e programação: desenvolvimento de sistemas, estruturas de dados e bancos de dados.

Aprendizado de máquina: criação e avaliação de modelos capazes de identificar padrões e realizar previsões a partir de dados.

Aprendizado profundo e inteligência artificial generativa: estudo de técnicas que permitem desenvolver sistemas mais complexos, incluindo aplicações de IA generativa.

Processamento de linguagem natural e visão computacional: métodos para que sistemas trabalhem com linguagem humana e informações visuais.

Engenharia de dados e processamento de dados massivos: organização e tratamento de grandes volumes de informações.

Inteligência artificial responsável: análise dos aspectos éticos e dos impactos das tecnologias.

A formação conta com Projetos Integradores, que serão desenvolvidos ao longo do curso. Neles, os estudantes aplicam os conhecimentos adquiridos a problemas reais, em contato com diferentes áreas e organizações.

Nos dois últimos semestres, também será possível aprofundar os estudos em uma de três ênfases:

Administração Pública e Governo Digital;

Estágio supervisionado e Trabalho de Conclusão de Curso (TCC) completam a graduação.

O bacharel poderá atuar no desenvolvimento e na aplicação de soluções baseadas em dados e inteligência artificial, em atividades como análise de grandes volumes de informações, criação de modelos de aprendizado de máquina, automação de processos e desenvolvimento de ferramentas para apoiar decisões.

empresas de tecnologia, startups e consultorias;

centros de pesquisa e organizações do terceiro setor.

A formação também prepara o egresso para atuar em pesquisa científica e desenvolvimento tecnológico, além de permitir a continuidade dos estudos em programas de pós-graduação no Brasil e no exterior.

Campus da Unicamp, em Limeira — Foto: Antoninho Perri/Unicamp

Relações Internacionais: entender o mundo e conectar desafios globais à realidade local

O bacharelado em Relações Internacionais será oferecido pela Faculdade de Ciências Aplicadas (FCA), também no campus de Limeira. A graduação busca formar profissionais capazes de compreender as dinâmicas políticas, econômicas e sociais que conectam países, empresas e instituições .

A proposta considera um cenário internacional marcado por disputas entre potências, mudanças nas cadeias produtivas, fluxos migratórios e desafios de segurança global. Também leva em conta a presença de multinacionais, polos industriais e centros de inovação no eixo Limeira–Piracicaba–Campinas.

A área reúne conhecimentos de diferentes campos, como ciência política, economia, direito, geopolítica e negócios internacionais . Essa combinação permite estudar desde a diplomacia e a cooperação entre países até o comércio exterior e os impactos das tecnologias digitais nas relações entre governos, mercados e sociedades.

A interdisciplinaridade é um dos princípios da formação. A grade curricular contempla temas fundamentais das Relações Internacionais, entre eles:

Teoria das relações internacionais: estudo dos conceitos e das abordagens que ajudam a compreender as relações entre países e outros atores globais.

Política externa comparada: análise das estratégias adotadas por diferentes países em suas relações com o exterior.

Economia política internacional: compreensão das conexões entre poder, economia e disputas globais.

Direito internacional público e privado: estudo das normas que orientam relações e acordos que ultrapassam fronteiras nacionais.

Diplomacia e negociação: desenvolvimento de conhecimentos para a mediação de interesses e a construção de acordos.

Segurança internacional: análise de conflitos, ameaças e novas agendas de segurança.

Integração regional, comércio exterior e governança global: estudo das relações econômicas e institucionais entre países.

A formação também aborda questões contemporâneas, como os limites do multilateralismo, as disputas geopolíticas por recursos estratégicos, as transformações nos regimes de comércio e os efeitos das tecnologias digitais nas relações internacionais.

A partir do quinto semestre, os estudantes passam a participar do Laboratório de Pesquisas em Relações Internacionais, que integra ensino, pesquisa e extensão. A proposta é aproximar as agendas locais e regionais das dinâmicas globais, por meio de projetos e atividades práticas.

Simulações de organismos multilaterais, projetos de extensão e parcerias com atores governamentais, empresariais e da sociedade civil também fazem parte da graduação.

O internacionalista poderá atuar em áreas ligadas à diplomacia, ao comércio exterior, às negociações internacionais e às relações institucionais.

órgãos governamentais e organismos multilaterais;

consultorias em relações governamentais e análise de risco político;

empresas com presença ou planos de expansão internacional.

Na prática, o profissional poderá elaborar análises estratégicas sobre cenários globais, gerir projetos e negócios internacionais, estruturar iniciativas de cooperação e captação de recursos junto a organismos internacionais e articular interesses locais em ambientes internacionais.

A formação ainda oferece base para quem pretende seguir carreira acadêmica e ingressar em programas de pós-graduação no Brasil ou no exterior.

Os candidatos interessados em conhecer os detalhes das duas graduações podem consultar o Catálogo de Graduação da Unicamp, disponível no site da Diretoria Acadêmica (DAC), e os respectivos projetos pedagógicos. Os documentos apresentam a estrutura completa dos cursos e permitem conhecer as disciplinas e a organização da formação ao longo dos semestres.

O Vestibular 2027 da Unicamp recebeu 58.431 inscrições para 2.523 vagas , distribuídas em 70 cursos de graduação.

O número de candidatos é 5,2% menor em relação ao ano anterior e o mais baixo registrado em uma década , segundo a Comissão Permanente para os Vestibulares (Comvest).

As provas serão realizadas no período da manhã, com início às 9h. A primeira fase está marcada para outubro, enquanto a segunda será aplicada em novembro. Confira o calendário:

articles.title: Apple lawyer to court in OpenAI theft case: We don’t need to check devices of all 400 former employees who joined ChatGPT-maker, as OpenAI knows who the...
articles.summary: Apple does not want to search the devices of every former employee who has moved to OpenAI.
articles.body: Apple does not want to search the devices of every former employee who has moved to OpenAI. That was the message from the iPhone maker’s lawyer at a federal court hearing in San Jose, California, on Wednesday, the first big showdown in Apple’s trade secrets lawsuit against the ChatGPT maker.US District Judge Edward Davila said he was “highly likely” to side with Apple and grant an injunction against OpenAI. Before he could rule, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use any information Apple says its former staff took, for as long as the case runs. According to Bloomberg, the judge can enforce that promise, which also requires OpenAI to collect forensic images of 14 employees’ devices.Apple narrows its OpenAI device inspection to a few ex-employeesDavila did not give Apple everything it wanted. He felt a proposed forensic inspection of every device and repository holding Apple trade secrets was too big an ask.Apple’s counsel John M. Desmarais said the company would only inspect a small group of employees who left for OpenAI. Hundreds of Apple staff have joined the AI company, but Desmarais told the judge OpenAI has “a few bad apples and know who they are.”The agreement spares OpenAI an outright loss in its first real courtroom test against Apple. The Cupertino company, meanwhile, gets most of what it was after: its proprietary information stays out of OpenAI’s product work.A day earlier, Davila had ordered OpenAI to fast-track evidence, including device images and LINE messages between former Apple engineers Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng, who had discussed wiping their Apple-owned devices. Liu, Peng and OpenAI hardware chief Tang Yew Tan must also sit for early depositions.OpenAI accuses a returning Apple engineer of taking its device filesOpenAI arrived at the hearing with allegations of its own. Hours earlier, it filed claims that an engineer who left Apple for OpenAI, then returned to Apple after about six months, sent more than 100 confidential files on at least one unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts.The files allegedly included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data, and supplier details. Some went out on June 2, his last day at OpenAI. He also allegedly presented OpenAI’s product plans to senior Apple executives, including its vice president of operations in Asia.Apple says it has policies that stop new hires from using a former employer’s confidential information, and that it has found no evidence supporting OpenAI’s claims. Reuters reported that in an October 12 letter, Apple’s lawyers noted the personal phone numbers OpenAI flagged do not match the one the engineer uses for Apple work. OpenAI wants time to investigate and may file counterclaims.What the Apple vs OpenAI lawsuit means for OpenAI’s first deviceApple sued in July, accusing OpenAI, Tan and Liu of a coordinated effort to extract details on product design, manufacturing, components, testing and the supply chain from former Apple staff. Tan spent over 24 years at Apple, where he was vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch.OpenAI denies the charges and says Apple is trying to stop employees from joining a rival. The two companies were partners not long ago, with ChatGPT built into Apple software since 2024, before Apple moved Siri to Google’s Gemini models.The timing matters for OpenAI, which is preparing to go public at a targeted $1.4 trillion valuation. Bloomberg has reported its first device will be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced above $300 (about Rs 26,400).Trial is expected in October 2027, though OpenAI says it could be ready as early as June 2027. Until then, the 14 devices it must image will show how far Apple’s “few bad apples” argument goes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.
articles.body:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly.

Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.

Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

articles.title: Anthropic Pitches AI Safety Bill to Lawmakers, Politico Says
articles.summary: Anthropic PBC has quietly presented its own draft AI safety bill to US lawmakers with a plan for regulating artificial intelligence safety and security, acco...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC has quietly presented its own draft AI safety bill to US lawmakers with a plan for regulating artificial intelligence safety and security, according to a Politico report.

According to Politico, the proposal suggests the government could block the release of an AI model if it's determined to imminently risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damages. The threat must be a result of the model creating or releasing a biological weapon, the AI going beyond human control or a cyberattack, Politico reported.

The bill also proposes that independent evaluators would routinely review Anthropic and its AI models, said Politico, citing a draft it had reviewed.

The draft proposes many of the the ideas Anthropic first proposed in its Advanced AI Framework this June.

The report did not specify which lawmakers or how broadly Anthropic has pitched the proposal so far.

articles.summary: Presidente dos EUA chegou a fazer enquetes para escolher um novo nome para a inteligência artificial. Especialistas veem motivações políticas na proposta.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, conversa com a imprensa antes de embarcar no helicóptero Marine One rumo a Grand Island, Nebraska — Foto: REUTERS/Eric Lee

O atual hiperfoco de Donald Trump é... a inteligência artificial 👀. O presidente dos Estados Unidos tem insistido que quer mudar o nome da tecnologia para "superinteligência (SI)".

Em seu discurso na Assembleia Geral da ONU , no mês passado, Trump afirmou que "o nome inteligência artificial faz soar como se ela fosse falsa". Disse ainda que "de agora em diante, todos os documentos dos EUA e, espero, de todo o mundo, vão utilizar o nome Superinteligência".

Antes de decidir por "Superinteligência", Trump chegou a abrir uma enquete em sua rede social , a Truth Social, com as opções "Inteligência Superior (IS)" , "Inteligência Extrema (IE)" e "Inteligência Suprema (IS)", traduzidas para o português.

Dois dias depois, ele fez uma nova enquete , desta vez com "Superinteligência" e "Inteligência Superior" . Em nenhuma das postagens, ele explicou como a alteração seria feita ou se o mercado de tecnologia concordava com a mudança.

E tem mais: em seguida, Trump causou polêmica ao afirmar que passaria a tratar como "inimigo" quem usasse o termo "inteligência artificial" em vez de "Superinteligência".

Quem não acompanha tecnologia talvez tenha ouvido falar de IA apenas recentemente, sobretudo com o surgimento do ChatGPT. Mas o conceito existe há mais de 70 anos e a tecnologia está presente no dia a dia há muito tempo, após passar por grandes transformações nas últimas décadas. (entenda mais abaixo)

Por isso, mudar o nome da IA não é tão simples quanto parece. Segundo Anderson Soares, considerado o brasileiro mais influente em IA , o próprio conceito de inteligência ainda não tem uma definição precisa, tanto nas ciências biológicas e naturais quanto no campo da tecnologia.

"O que chamamos hoje de inteligência artificial está relacionado à capacidade das máquinas de realizar tarefas que associamos à inteligência humana", afirma Soares, que também é fundador e professor do Centro de Excelência em Inteligência Artificial (CEIA), da Universidade Federal de Goiás (UFG).

"O objetivo de mudar o nome me parece muito mais um contragolpe na questão de paralisar o desenvolvimento da IA . Parece mais um ato político do que efetivamente algo construtivo e que contribua para o que está acontecendo em termos de desenvolvimento", completa.

ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude, Mistral AI, Gemini, Copilot e Poe — Foto: Solen Feyissa/Unsplash

Cleber Zanchettin, professor de Engenharia da Computação da Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE) e especialista em IA, chama a atenção para o discurso de Trump na ONU.

"Primeiro, ele disse 'bem-vindos ao novo mundo da superinteligência' e completou com 'vamos ver se isso vai dar certo'. Isso revela uma jogada de marketing para chamar atenção, sem efeito prático", disse.

Para o professor e pesquisador Allan Pscheidt, a proposta de Trump também não parece ser uma mudança na definição científica ou técnica da tecnologia, mas uma demonstração de poder e soberania dos EUA no cenário internacional de IA.

"A gente está vivendo algo parecido com o que aconteceu na corrida para a Lua e na corrida espacial. Estamos passando agora para a corrida pela AGI (Inteligência Artificial Geral)", diz Pscheidt.

"Quando Trump vem com a ideia de cunhar o termo 'superinteligência', ele está avisando ao mundo que os EUA vão atingir a AGI muito em breve e que, com isso, vão mostrar sua soberania tecnológica", afirma.

🔎 AGI (sigla em inglês para "Inteligência Artificial Geral") é o termo usado para descrever uma IA capaz de realizar uma ampla variedade de tarefas intelectuais em nível semelhante ou superior ao dos humanos. Allan ressalta que, até o momento, não há comprovação científica de que já exista uma superinteligência.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump (no centro), durante reunião na Casa Branca com líderes de empresas de IA, como Meta, Nvidia, Google e xAI, em 29 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Jonathan Ernst/ Reuters

Cleber Zanchettin, da UFPE, alerta que, como grande parte da população ainda tem pouco conhecimento sobre tecnologia, produtos com o rótulo de IA já enfrentam certa rejeição ou medo no mercado.

"Introduzir um termo como 'superinteligência' ou 'inteligência suprema' pode soar como uma ameaça aos humanos e aumentar a rejeição do público", explica Zanchettin.

"Poucos países e populações abraçaram a tecnologia de fato, e a maioria das pessoas ainda está tentando entender o que é a IA básica e como ela funciona".

Mais da metade dos brasileiros (52%) diz estar mais preocupada do que animada com o avanço da inteligência artificial , segundo uma pesquisa recente do Pew Research Center.

Nos EUA, a percepção é semelhante: cerca de nove em cada 10 americanos dizem estar mais preocupados do que animados com a possibilidade de a IA um dia superar a inteligência humana, segundo uma pesquisa da CNN divulgada em setembro.

Um caderno manuscrito de 56 páginas que pertenceu ao pioneiro da computação Alan Turing é leiloado em Nova York — Foto: REUTERS/Bobby Yip

O termo IA nasceu do trabalho de pesquisadores de diferentes áreas, como engenharia, matemática e estatística. Eles buscavam entender como criar máquinas capazes de demonstrar alguma forma de raciocínio e inteligência semelhante à dos seres humanos, explicou Zanchettin.

O nome foi definido formalmente em meados de 1955, nos Estados Unidos, e surgiu do trabalho de pesquisadores como John McCarthy , Marvin Minsky , Claude Shannon e Nathaniel Rochester, explicou o professor.

"Eles precisavam de uma nomenclatura para pesquisas que misturavam matemática, engenharia e estatística para criar máquinas capazes de exibir raciocínio, algo que não se enquadrava no software tradicional da época", disse Zanchettin.

Mas as pesquisas sobre máquinas capazes de pensar começaram antes disso. Entre as décadas de 1940 e 1950, o matemático e cientista da computação Alan Turing já estudava essa possibilidade, explica o pesquisador Allan Pscheidt.

Na mesma época, em 1948, o matemático Norbert Wiener criou o termo "cibernética" para estudar sistemas capazes de usar informações sobre suas próprias ações para ajustar seu funcionamento.

Segundo Pscheidt, foi nesse contexto que John McCarthy criou a expressão "inteligência artificial", em 1955. A escolha também buscava diferenciar esse campo de pesquisa da cibernética, com foco no raciocínio e na autonomia das máquinas.

Com o avanço e a popularização da tecnologia, a IA passou a fazer parte do cotidiano das pessoas, em recursos como reconhecimento facial de bancos , carros semiautônomos , drones , alto-falantes inteligentes e câmeras de celulares .

Mais recentemente, a partir de 2017, ganhou força a IA generativa, que deu origem a ferramentas como o ChatGPT e é capaz de criar textos, imagens, vídeos e músicas.

No fim, para Anderson Soares, "as ondas tecnológicas costumam passar por fases relativamente previsíveis: primeiro provocam medo e desconfiança; depois vêm a aceitação e o encantamento; e, com o tempo, a tecnologia passa a ser compreendida e deixa de parecer algo extraordinário".

articles.title: The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
articles.summary: Experts say balancing the need to govern AI for public safety with user privacy is ‘extraordinarily difficult’.
articles.body:
For months before carrying out Canada’s deadliest school shooting in almost four decades, Jesse Van Rootselaar was consulting an unlikely adviser on how to perpetrate mass murder.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 [Remington shotgun] is brutal … Close quarters is its playground,” OpenAI’s ChatGPT guided the 18-year-old, according to reports.

On February 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar shot his mother and half-brother at home before going to a school in the small British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, where he killed another six people – including five students – before taking his own life.

Earlier this week, on October 14, US authorities charged a Washington State man with allegedly conspiring with Van Rootselaar to plan the attack. But the mass shooting incident has raised questions that go beyond the traditional legal understanding of culpability.

The British Columbia government in September filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, accusing them of failing to prevent the incident and claiming they were aware of the conversations that turned deadly. Families of the victims also filed separate lawsuits. OpenAI’s leadership issued a public apology for their failure to notify authorities.

The company has not responded to requests from Al Jazeera for its comments on the lawsuits.

But as the case against OpenAI progresses, it has spurred a familiar debate: Where should a line be drawn between reporting potentially dangerous behaviour and protecting an individual’s privacy?

“The question of whether companies should be required to turn such information over to law enforcement is extraordinarily difficult, particularly if they don’t already screen chats for indications of such types of threats,” United States-based civil liberties lawyer Jenin Younes told Al Jazeera.

“Forcing companies to implement a surveillance system implicates very serious civil liberties concerns, and that’s probably a bridge too far for me,” Younes added.

“On the other hand, AI gives individuals access to types and quantities of information they didn’t have previously that may facilitate the commission of mass casualty events, a concern it’s not easy to dismiss.”

AI’s ability to distinguish thoughts from threats

One of the biggest challenges facing AI companies is determining whether a user expressing violent thoughts actually intends to act on them.

In August, Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, flagged a user to San Francisco police after discovering conversations allegedly threatening its CEO, Dario Amodei.

According to the San Francisco Standard, citing a police report, the user had claimed to possess an AR-15 gun and suggested he had Amodei “in his sights”.

However, when contacted by the newspaper, the man said he was joking and had no intention of carrying out any form of violence. The person was neither charged nor detained, the Standard said.

Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, said current AI models cannot “reliably” determine whether an interaction with an AI chatbot “is purely hypothetical or is likely to lead to harmful behaviour”.

“Suppose you are a creative writer working on a fictional story and want to explore how a murder plot might unfold. From the context, it may be clear that this is simply a fictional narrative. If the threshold for flagging potentially harmful content is too low, such a writer could be wrongly flagged,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Similarly, consider a graduate student in biology or chemistry studying pathogens that, if misused, could have serious consequences. They might be trying to understand the risks associated with these pathogens and how to mitigate them. Such discussions may be necessary for legitimate research and education. Even when the subject matter is sensitive, they should not automatically be flagged without considering the broader context.”

The researcher said identifying a credible threat may require examining a user’s interactions across multiple conversations, rather than relying on isolated statements.

Barez said someone experiencing intrusive violent thoughts might turn to a chatbot for support, while another person planning an attack may reveal their intentions gradually across several conversations.

“Distinguishing between the two requires careful consideration of context, intent and patterns of behaviour, rather than relying on individual statements alone,” he added.

Chinmayi Sharma, a law professor at Fordham University, said the debate has parallels with the duty imposed on mental health professionals to warn identifiable third parties about credible threats.

However, she said there was a key difference – therapists have professional training, knowledge of their patients and enforceable standards governing their conduct. AI companies do not necessarily have comparable safeguards.

“My concern with AI companies is that right now there’s not a concerted effort to hire mental health professionals, sociologists, individuals that would have the unique expertise on what the indicators of threat are here,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.

“Secondly, licensed professionals are accountable to concrete, legally enforceable standards in their discipline. We don’t have something like that for AI companies.”

The privacy implications extend beyond whether AI companies can accurately identify threats. Millions of people use chatbots to discuss relationships, emotional distress, mental health concerns and deeply personal experiences.

Civil liberties lawyer Younes said many users may not realise how vulnerable those conversations could be to disclosure.

“They often reflect a person’s innermost thoughts, questions, and desires. The majority of people assume that these dialogues will never be viewed by another person,” Younes, president and legal director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, said.

Younes warned that the consequences of greater monitoring could extend well beyond those planning violence.

“If people fear their chats can be turned over to law enforcement simply because they express disturbing thoughts/violent fantasies etc, many will be dissuaded from using them,” she told Al Jazeera.

Younes argued that forcing companies to establish systems for monitoring users and reporting conversations could raise serious constitutional concerns in the US, including protections against unreasonable searches.

Meanwhile, Fordham’s Sharma also raised an issue about who could be disproportionately affected by heavy monitoring by AI chatbots.

“The concern is always there about either intentional or unintentional targeting, because if you have models trained on what we consider dangerous speech, they’re almost always going to reflect biases,” she said. “Certain minorities’ speech is over‑flagged as a threat, while other comparable speech is not.

“Even in a world in which everyone is benevolent, we should still be concerned about disparate outcomes,” she said, warning that machines could reproduce such disparities at scale.

‘Not a licensed therapist’ – When do AI companies become liable to report?

While AI companies may face moral pressure to prevent violence, their legal obligations are less clear, legal experts say.

Bryan Choi, a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, said US law recognises a duty to warn in certain circumstances, including when mental health professionals become aware of imminent threats or when a special relationship exists between parties.

But those principles do not necessarily apply to AI companies.

“Under present case law, it seems unlikely that a company such as OpenAI would be held to have such duties to warn,” Choi told Al Jazeera. “The chatbot is not a licensed therapist. There is no special relationship between the company and the victims.”

Choi said existing negligence and product liability laws could potentially be applied to AI companies, but proving responsibility would present significant challenges.

Fordham’s Sharma suggested that independent institutions could help establish reporting standards rather than leaving decisions entirely to private companies or requiring immediate disclosure to police.

Such bodies she said could develop procedures for assessing threats and explore ways of sharing only relevant information while protecting users’ identities and other personal details.

Meanwhile, Younes argued that users should, at a minimum, be clearly informed about whether their conversations are monitored and what circumstances could lead to information being shared with law enforcement.

“This is almost certainly an issue that will be wrestled with over the coming years, and I’m not sure anyone knows the solution at this particular point in time,” she said.

“Events that have not yet occurred will likely influence how these policies are shaped.”

articles.title: A 44-minute call and a memo: How Alexandr Wang won Mark Zuckerberg’s trust—and a $100 billion-plus AI bet
articles.summary: Meta’s CEO and his 29-year-old chief AI officer revealed on Stripe cofounder John Collison’s podcast how one phone call became Meta Superintelligence Labs, a...
articles.body:
Mark Zuckerberg once poured tens of billions of dollars into a metaverse that few people wanted to live in. Now he's spending even more on Muse , Meta's personal AI agent—the kind of assistant that, in Zuckerberg's case, coaches his MMA form between rounds and, in Alexandr Wang's, hunts down obscure loose-leaf teas from farms in Taiwan and Japan.

Those are a couple of the favorite use cases of Zuckerberg and Wang, the 29-year-old MIT dropout and Scale AI cofounder Zuckerberg tapped last year to lead Meta Superintelligence Labs. The Muse app launched in the U.S. on Sept. 8 and quickly became the most popular free app on Apple's App Store, topping 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN . On Monday, Meta followed up with Muse Wonder , the first model from the lab that Meta calls frontier-class.

"We're going to write this check for like, I don't know, like $100 billion or $200 billion," Zuckerberg said of discussions late last year, appearing alongside Wang on the latest episode of Cheeky Pint , the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. "I'm like, Alex, you sure this is going to work?"

The figure was off the cuff, but the scale is real. Meta now expects 2026 capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion , nearly double the $72.2 billion it spent last year—and investors have flinched at each increase.

Wang said he heard a version of Zuckerberg's question from Meta's CFO, Susan Li, at an executive gathering in Hawaii at the end of last year. "Susan pulled me aside many times," Wang said. "I just want to tell you if this doesn't work, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms. I really need to impress on you that this model has to work. It has to be good. If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad."

Between sips of Guinness—a moment of apparent wincing by Zuckerberg went viral —the pair recounted how their partnership began. In April 2025, shortly after Meta's Llama 4 models landed to a lukewarm reception, Zuckerberg started reaching out for advice. ( Fortune previously reported that the two began spending more time together that month.) Wang was in a staff meeting when his phone pinged. "I got the WhatsApp notification, like, 'Have time for a call?'" Wang said. "I was like, huh, interesting."

That call ran about 44 minutes, by Zuckerberg's recollection. Two days later, Wang sent him a long memo laying out, as Zuckerberg put it, "here's what I think I would do if I were in your position."

articles.title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
articles.summary: OpenAI, Meta, Google, and others are positioning AI agents as personal assistants that can perform a range of tasks online. But the web is becoming increasingly unfriendly toward agents, undermining their usefulness.
articles.body: Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice? In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them. Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.” Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint. This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are. “Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.” Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents. The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment. Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.” The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products. While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

articles.title: DeepSeek Pushes Out Updated AI Model It Says Is Faster, Leaner
articles.summary: DeepSeek released an update of its AI model this weekend that it says is faster and leaner, ramping up the Chinese company’s challenge to Silicon Valley riva...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- DeepSeek released an update of its AI model this weekend that it says is faster and leaner, ramping up the Chinese company's challenge to Silicon Valley rivals Anthropic PBC and OpenAI as well as domestic competitors like Moonshot Kimi and Z.ai

The firm unveiled the V4.1-Flash-1017 late Saturday afternoon with a series of posts on X saying the update had "stronger benchmark performance, faster task completion, and shorter outputs than the previous version." The model is live across the web, on DeepSeek's app and its platform for developers.

The rapid pace of DeepSeek's new launches underscores the intensifying contest between China's open-weight models and the proprietary models of their US counterparts, which are top performers, but with far higher costs.

DeepSeek's latest iteration delivers "substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks," the Hangzhou-based startup said in its technical report on Hugging Face, the online platform for AI models, data sets and apps.

The model released Saturday improves capabilities in uses ranging from game creation to 3D modeling. The company described the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 as a minor update to its earlier V4.1-Flash.

Earlier this week, DeepSeek suffered an outage of about five hours, leaving its servers unreachable. Some experts attributed the glitch to a lack of sufficient computing resources. Slowdowns and service disruptions have increased in recent months for DeepSeek, whose aggressively priced AI models are sought after by developers, putting pressure on its services.

Saturday's model update was preceded by the slimmed down V4.1-Flash AI system, unveiled early in September. DeepSeek offered it at such a steep discount that shares of rivals such as MiniMax Group Inc., Z.ai and even the giant Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., which is driving its Qwen models, plummeted on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

The latest update seeks to be a stronger, faster and more compact version of its predecessor.

DeepSeek disclosed benchmarking scores for its latest update on X. On Humanity's Last Exam, the revised model scored 36.8 to 42.6, an improvement on V4.1-Flash, which scored 36.8 to 39.1. HLE, as it's known, measures how AI models perform on thousands of questions in math, sciences and humanities.

articles.title: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
articles.summary: Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms.
articles.body: After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page: > … Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file. Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning: > “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

articles.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
articles.summary: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
articles.body:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

articles.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
articles.body:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

articles.title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
articles.body:
Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab , this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)

However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

articles.body:
Alunos realizam 1ª fase do vestibular da Unicamp em salas de aula na PUC Campinas — Foto: Thomaz Marostegan/g1

A primeira fase do vestibular 2027 da Unicamp , realizada neste domingo (18), abordou a política indigenista durante a ditadura militar , o conceito de democracia , desinformação sobre a vacina da Covid-19 causar Aids, análise sobre quantos estadunidenses apoiam ou não as deportações e a propagação da linguagem nas redes sociais com a gíria "gag" .

Hillary Stephany Vila Ramos de Aquino, de 19 anos, que prestou para engenharia elétrica e engenharia de alimentos, avaliou a prova como "complicadinha", mas destacou a questão sobre a gíria em inglês "gag", que significa ficar totalmente chocado ou impressionado com alguma coisa .

"Achei superlegal. Não sabia que iria ter alguma coisa assim", comentou.

Entre os temas abordados, também houve análise de um texto que trabalha sobre a ideia de que o brasileiro trabalha pouco, o aspecto transgressor entre arte e política, capacidade de resignificação das palavras e uma menção ao primeiro vestibular da Unicamp, em 1987 .

Na avaliação de José Alves de Freitas Neto, diretor da Comissão Permanente para os Vestibulares (Comvest), da Unicamp, a prova seguiu a tendência dos últimos anos, com foco nas discussões do mundo contemporâneo.

"Voltamos a falar de negacionismo e ciência, voltamos a falar de ditadura e políticas indigenistas, falamos também do que está na boca do povo, a molecada, falando dos usos e da linguagem, o "gag", por exemplo, que apareceu na prova de inglês e como isso vai ter uma difusão via rede social", disse.

Para Mateus Clemente, de 18 anos, a prova foi cansativa, com muitas questões com enunciados extensos. Para ele, o destaque foi a presença de uma questão de abordou a cultura indígena, relacionada a uma fruta.

Já para Murillo Dias Gindanego, de 18 anos, que tenta uma vaga em engenharia química, a prova foi mais complexa do que imaginava, uma vez que focou mais em exatas do que em humanas. Segundo ele, a prova abordou a obra de Conceição Evaristo.

Segundo Clayton Alves Pereira, de 40 anos, funcionário público de Capivari (SP), e que sonha com uma vaga em arquitetura, a prova também trouxe uma questão relacionada a Inteligência Artificial (IA) e a relação entre EUA e China.

articles.title: Óculos com Inteligência Artificial dão autonomia a cegos em MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Dezesseis moradores de Araxá, no Alto Paranaíba, foram beneficiados pelo projeto criado há 6 meses. Os equipamentos ajudam os usuários em tarefas diárias, como escolher roupas ou fazer ligações.
articles.summary: Projeto em Araxá doa óculos com Inteligência Artificial para garantir autonomia e inclusão de pessoas com deficiência visual em diversas atividades do cotidiano.
articles.body:
Ana Flávia e a irmã Ana Paula são gêmeas e tem apenas 5% da visão. — Foto: Instituto InteliGENTE/ Divulgação

Óculos equipados com câmeras e Inteligência Artificial estão ajudando deficientes visuais de Araxá , no Alto Paranaíba, a terem mais autonomia em atividades diárias. Os equipamentos foram doados por um projeto criado por empresários e instituições da cidade há seis meses.

Dezesseis pessoas cegas ou com baixa visão já foram beneficiadas pela iniciativa. Os óculos têm câmeras e alto-falantes, que fazem parte da armação dos óculos, aliados a um sistema de IA.

A câmera capta o que está à frente da pessoa e a Inteligência Artificial analisa a imagem, identifica objetos, textos e ambientes. As informações são analisadas e transmitidas em áudio pelos alto-falantes, permitindo que o usuário ouça a descrição do que está à sua frente.

Os óculos também têm microfones, que permitem que o usuário faça perguntas por voz.

Uma das beneficiadas pelo projeto, Ana Paula de Oliveira, de 35 anos, diz que a tecnologia mudou a rotina dela e da irmã. As duas têm apenas 5% da visão.

“Os óculos se tornaram meu melhor amigo. Me ajudam até a escolher a roupa que vou usar, e também uso para fazer ligações, conversar com meu namorado e em outros momentos do meu dia”, contou a dona de casa.

No projeto, empresários se juntam para arrecadar o recurso necessário para a compra e doação dos óculos. Cada equipamento é adquirido, em média, por R$ 3 mil reais.

Wellington Martins, dono de uma escola de ensino profissional e técnico, em Araxá, é o idealizador da ação. Ele criou um instituto, que reúne parceiros dispostos a financiar a iniciativa.

Segundo o empresário, a ideia de ajudar pessoas com deficiência visual surgiu na década de 1980, quando ele tinha 13 anos e era guia de pessoas cegas em Araxá.

“Minha mãe também tem baixa visão e desde criança eu percebi a importância de pessoas com deficiência poderem ser independentes, empreendedoras e autônomas. E com o passar do tempo, percebi que a tecnologia poderia ajudar muito nisso. Os óculos com Inteligência Artificial conseguem auxiliar em inúmeras funções, promovendo inclusão e transformando a rotina dessas pessoas”, disse.

Quem já recebeu a doação dos óculos conta que os dispositivos representam mais independência e ajudam no aprendizado e na socialização. Luiz Eduardo Machado, de 29 anos, é deficiente visual e está concluindo o curso técnico de contabilidade.

Ele diz que, sem os óculos, a oportunidade de se formar seria praticamente impossível.

“Os óculos estão me ajudando a ler os livros, fazer os trabalhos propostos pelos professores e também no convívio com os colegas na sala de aula. Sem esse equipamento, eu não conseguiria chegar até aqui”, disse o estudante.

articles.title: Microsoft Scraps UK Data Center Deal With Nscale, Telegraph Says
articles.summary: Microsoft Corp. has pulled out of a UK data center deal with British neocloud Nscale at a critical time for the startup’s initial public offering hopes, the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. has pulled out of a UK data center deal with British neocloud Nscale at a critical time for the startup's initial public offering hopes, the Telegraph reported.

The newspaper did not provide a specific reason for why the US tech giant had pulled the plug on the deal in Loughton, Essex, though it said the site has been contending with a series of delays. Authorities have told Nscale they don't expect a power supply to the facility until the 2030s, it added.

Nscale's flagship site in Norway is also six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts of the intended 30-megawatt data center up and running.

Nscale relies on Microsoft and Anthropic for around 85% of its contracts, according to an IPO filing, and the former had been set to become the anchor tenant at Nscale's first British data center in Essex.

Microsoft's withdrawal would mark a setback for the company that's seeking to raise as much as $3 billion in an IPO as soon as this month, and which was already contending with investor jitters over the risks of the wider artificial intelligence buildout.

Nscale is one of the most prominent neoclouds, a new group of companies seeking to build huge computer complexes for AI. They want to cash in on the hundreds of billions of dollars big tech companies have pledged to spend on the technology and are a key part of the AI boom's supply chain.

An Nscale spokesman told the Telegraph: "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.

"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts."

Microsoft did not comment to the Telegraph and did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Bloomberg outside usual business hours.

The backdrop to Nscale's IPO ambitions has turned gloomier in recent days, with fellow neocloud CoreWeave Inc. in the spotlight last week after the co-founder said the company was exploring ways to borrow in investment-grade debt markets, where there are vast pools of money from insurers to tap.

articles.title: We didn’t protect children from social media — we have another chance with AI
articles.summary: The question is not whether children will grow up with artificial intelligence. They will. The question is whether, this time, we will build the research, safeguards and scientific guidance needed to understand what AI is doing to children — while we still have the opportunity to shape what comes next.
articles.body:
Earlier this year, Meta reached a landmark settlement with state attorneys general , agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion, subject to court approval, and make sweeping changes to how Facebook and Instagram operate for young users. The settlement followed years of mounting evidence, whistleblower disclosures, lawsuits and testimony from families about the effects social media can have on children.

It is tempting to see this as progress. It is progress. But it is also an indictment of how we got here.

For years, children used products engineered to capture and hold their attention while researchers worked to understand what those products were doing to sleep, mental health, relationships, learning and development . Families were repeatedly told to manage the risks themselves. Scientists accumulated evidence. Parents raised alarms. And eventually, after millions of children had already been exposed, safeguards began catching up.

We should not repeat that sequence with artificial intelligence.

In an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper , Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang argued that AI safety is fundamentally an engineering challenge. If an AI product is unsafe, he said, companies should simply refrain from releasing it. Better containment, monitoring and technical safeguards can address the risks.

Days earlier, in a conversation with Ezra Klein , Huang confronted another kind of risk. Klein cited research involving more than 26,000 secondary-school students in China that found generative AI use improved homework performance and reduced the time spent completing assignments, but was associated with lower exam scores within six months.

Huang acknowledged that children are already forgetting skills such as long division and multiplication tables. His response was essentially to ask whether that matters. Humanity has always stopped memorizing certain things when technology made those skills unnecessary, he argued. We may lose some forms of intellectual dexterity and develop others.

Maybe. Technology has always changed what humans need to know. But Huang and others are investing in AI precisely because it promises change at a speed and scale that far exceeds previous technologies. This time, we do not yet know what we may lose, what we may gain, or whether children will emerge stronger or weaker as a result.

Childhood should not be optimized for ease or efficiency. It should be optimized for growth. The point of learning is not simply to produce the right answer as quickly as possible. Struggling with a problem, tolerating frustration, retrieving information from memory, evaluating whether something makes sense, generating an original idea, and learning how to communicate with another human being are developmental experiences. When technology performs those tasks for a child, we need to understand what is being gained, what is being displaced, and whether those tradeoffs differ at age eight, 13 and 17.

And learning is only one part of childhood that AI is beginning to reshape.

Children and teenagers are already turning to conversational systems for companionship, emotional reassurance and advice. A 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 12 percent of U.S. teens had used AI chatbots for emotional support or advice. Some of these systems are designed to offer personalized, emotionally responsive interactions that can make them especially compelling to young users. For a lonely adolescent, that can make an AI interaction unusually appealing.

That does not mean AI is inherently bad for children. Generative AI could become an extraordinary support. It may help children explore ideas, overcome barriers to learning, express creativity and access knowledge in ways we are only beginning to understand. It may also help young people rehearse difficult conversations or find appropriate sources of support when they need them.

But “it might help” and “we can fix problems later” cannot be our entire child-safety framework.

Scientists are increasingly saying the same thing. A recent international study involving 272 AI experts identified risks ranging from misinformation and overreliance to dangerous capabilities and competitive pressures among developers. Other researchers are beginning to map how generative AI could affect children’s cognitive, emotional and social development , finding that outcomes may depend heavily on age, intensity of use, system design, adult involvement and what AI interactions replace in a child’s life.

An AI tutor that helps a teenager work through a difficult equation is different from one that supplies the answer. A chatbot used to brainstorm a story is different from one that writes it. A tool that encourages a distressed child to talk with a trusted adult is different from one designed to become the child’s trusted confidant itself.

Yet products are evolving faster than our ability to study these differences.

Before AI becomes inseparable from childhood, we should build the scientific infrastructure needed to understand its effects while there is still time to shape them. That means investing aggressively in independent research that follows children over time and giving researchers access to data that allows them to evaluate how specific AI features affect learning, relationships, emotional development, mental health and behavior. Developers should work with experts in child development before products reach millions of young users, rather than after harms appear. Safety evaluations should ask developmentally specific questions instead of treating a 10-year-old as a smaller version of an adult.

Children and Screens recently joined researchers across child development, neuroscience, psychology, education and digital safety to map the emerging evidence around generative AI and children. One conclusion was unavoidable: the effects will depend on what we build. Which future we get will be shaped by choices being made now.

The question is not whether children will grow up with artificial intelligence. They will. The question is whether, this time, we will build the research, safeguards and scientific guidance needed to understand what AI is doing to children — while we still have the opportunity to shape what comes next.

Kris Perry is executive director of Children and Screens.

IREN (NasdaqGS:IREN) is drawing fresh scrutiny as it expands its AI data center business with substantial short term financial commitments.

Analysts are highlighting funding risks tied to higher capital expenditures for AI infrastructure under tighter credit conditions and rising financing costs.
